general.title_original: Thailand rallies designers to take Chud Thai to the world
general.summary_original:
BANGKOK — Thailand’s Ministry of Culture is bringing together leading designers, fashion houses and textile businesses to promote traditional Thai national dress as both a cultural heritage and a driver of the country’s creative economy.

Culture Minister Sabida Thaiseth met with prominent Thai designers and fashion houses on Sunday to discuss ways to promote Chud Thai Phra Ratchaniyom, or royal Thai dress, and the royal-style shirt for men while preserving their traditional identity.

The ministry said correctly designed and tailored Thai dress can create demand for locally produced textiles, including silk, cotton, brocade and regional fabrics, with economic benefits reaching weavers, farmers, artisans and communities.

Sabida said Thai national dress is distinctive for its intricate tailoring and craftsmanship, combining traditional textile patterns with contemporary design.

The eight styles of Chud Thai Phra Ratchaniyom were developed after Queen Sirikit studied historical Thai women’s clothing and commissioned designs for official overseas visits in 1960. For men, King Bhumibol Adulyadej introduced the royal-style Thai shirt in 1980 as an alternative to Western formal wear, particularly suited to Thailand’s climate.

The styles have since evolved in terms of design, materials and textile techniques, while becoming widely recognized as part of Thailand’s national identity.

The Department of Cultural Promotion listed Chud Thai Phra Ratchaniyom as a national intangible cultural heritage item in 2023 under social practices, rituals, traditions and festivals.

In March 2024, the Cabinet approved Thailand’s nomination of “Chud Thai: The Knowledge, Craftsmanship and Practices of the Thai National Costume” for UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

UNESCO has confirmed that the nomination will be considered at the 21st session of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, scheduled for December 2026.

Sabida said the meeting with designers and fashion houses was an opportunity to exchange ideas and expertise on maintaining the authenticity of Thai dress while adapting it to different body types, occasions and contemporary tastes.

She said traditional styles can be creatively adapted without losing their identity. For example, the Chud Thai Ruean Ton can be paired with different types of traditional textiles, from silk and cotton to distinctive local and ethnic fabrics.

The ministry is promoting the campaign “CHUD THAI” to bring Thai dress to international audiences while encouraging designers and the public to incorporate Thai craftsmanship into everyday life.

The campaign also aims to expand markets for Thai textiles and handicrafts and strengthen the international image of Thailand’s creative industries ahead of UNESCO’s consideration of the nomination in December.

general.title_original: Buriram monks brawl after argument over temple pickup truck
general.summary_original:
BURIRAM — 24 August 2026, A newly ordained monk and a senior monk got into a fistfight at a temple in Buriram after arguing over the use of a pickup truck to transport rocks for repairs around the temple grounds.

The newly ordained monk suffered a cut below his left eye that required four stitches and later filed a police report.

Local residents took 21-year-old Anusorn, a monk at Tha Sawang Temple in Krasang subdistrict, Krasang district, to Krasang Hospital after he was injured by a sharp object below his left eye.

Doctors stitched the wound four times before releasing him back to the temple.

When asked about the incident, Anusorn said he had only recently been ordained for the Buddhist Lent period. After noticing several potholes around the temple grounds, he asked an older monk, whom he referred to as “Luang Ta,” for the keys to a temple pickup truck so he could collect rocks to repair the area.

However, the senior monk refused and suggested that he use a handcart instead, saying the distance was not far and that using the truck would waste fuel.

Anusorn admitted that the response angered him. The two then became involved in a heated argument in the middle of the temple grounds.

As tensions boiled over, Anusorn said he lost his temper and threw the first punch at the senior monk’s face. The senior monk then punched him back in self-defense.

The fight quickly turned into a scuffle, shocking relatives and laypeople who witnessed the incident. They intervened and took Anusorn to hospital after seeing blood covering his face.

In addition to the wound below his eye, Anusorn suffered abrasions on his right arm. He said he had since filed a police report at Krasang Police Station.

The senior monk, identified as 50-year-old Santathu Worawuttho, had bruising on his face.

He said he had been a monk for 11 years and believed his suggestion to use a handcart was reasonable.

Instead, he said Anusorn responded angrily, saying, “It’s not your truck. Why are you so protective of it?”

Santathu said Anusorn attacked him first, prompting him to put a rock in his hand and punch Anusorn in the face. The two then became involved in a physical fight until residents stepped in to separate them.

The temple abbot and senior monks are now preparing to establish a disciplinary committee to investigate both monks and determine appropriate action under monastic rules and Buddhist discipline.

general.title_original: Thai Army seeks drone warfare centre, armored vehicles, M777s and HIMARS
general.summary_original:
BANGKOK — The Royal Thai Army has proposed acquiring new military equipment, including wheeled armored vehicles, M777 howitzers and HIMARS rocket systems, as part of efforts to strengthen its operational readiness amid changing security threats.

The proposals were disclosed Monday following a visit by Defense Minister Adul Boonthamcharoen to Army headquarters, where he received briefings on the Army’s missions, operational challenges and plans to improve its capabilities.

Maj. Gen. Wintai Suvaree, an Army spokesman, said the Army had proposed updating its equipment, systems and regulations to respond to changing forms of threats. It also wants to modernize intelligence capabilities through greater cooperation with foreign countries.

The Army also proposed restructuring units responsible for aerial operations, including the establishment of an Unmanned Aerial Warfare Centre, or an unmanned aircraft battalion, to support its missions.

Among the equipment proposed for procurement are wheeled armored vehicles, supporting firepower, M777 155mm howitzers and HIMARS multiple rocket launchers. The proposals have been presented to the defense minister for consideration.

The Army has also requested additional funding to improve its capabilities, infrastructure and personnel.

The defense minister, meanwhile, emphasized that frontline military operations remain important but said information warfare conducted both domestically and internationally also poses a growing challenge.

He called for stronger coordination of military communications through a single official source, similar to the Joint Information Center (JIC) used to provide updates on the Thailand-Cambodia situation.

The approach is intended to provide the public with continuous, reliable information and reduce the impact of misleading claims circulating on social media.

The minister also urged the Army to adopt more proactive communication and encourage the public to rely on official sources when following security-related developments.
